items.summary: The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule targeting foreign remote access to advanced computing chips, including Nvidia's Blackwell. The measure addresses growing concerns that rapid advances in cloud computing and superintelligence infrastructure now make it feasible for countries subject to export restrictions—such as China, Russia and Iran—to obtain the most advanced artificial intelligence chips through data centres located outside their borders. Previously, these nations could circumvent US bans by renting access from overseas facilities rather than purchasing directly from firms like Nvidia. The new rule requires overseas data centres to conduct due diligence on customers and restricts those supplying significant volumes of computing power to companies headquartered in high-risk countries. It will also undermine the ability of such entities to use US chips to train advanced AI models, and it goes into effect 90 days after issuance. Under the provision, a license becomes required to export advanced chips to companies with headquarters in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil—nations identified as carrying an elevated risk of smuggling. The rule follows alleged spying connected to Nvidia; US investigators examined whether Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud company, helped Chinese clients access export-controlled Nvidia chips. Jensen Huang, the Nvidia co-founder who stepped down as CEO last week after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang—a former Megaspeed executive suspected of spying for China—was central to this scrutiny. Megaspeed rejected allegations that it sent chips to China. The move arrives just days before President Donald Trump is scheduled to travel to China for an economic summit, where he will meet his counterpart Xi Jinping.
items.title: US Clamps Down on Chip 'Loophole' in Foreign Access to Advanced AI Chips

items.summary: Reserve Bank board members who voted against this month's official interest rate hike warned they feared a 'materially sharper downturn' in the economy, arguing it was prudent to wait and see how higher borrowing costs would affect households. The three dissenting members of the nine-member board placed less weight on upside inflation risks and more on downside growth risks, pointing to rising unemployment as a concern. Meanwhile, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said she remained more worried about persistently high inflation than rising unemployment, warning that businesses were beginning to treat rapid price rises as the 'new normal'—with some thinking 3% or 3.5% might be acceptable—which could make it harder to bring inflation back down to target without further damaging rate hikes. Westpac economists said official figures would show consumer prices jumping to 4.8% in the year to October, from 4.3%, and rising to the highest since September 2023. Inflation has been above 3% for most of the past five years and is not expected to return to the central bank's 2.5% target until mid-2028. Federal treasurer Jim Chalmers, facing pressure over the government's economic strategy amid a stressed electorate entering summer, said next month's mid-year budget update 'will cut enough, but not too much' as savings would be its main focus amid intensifying spending pressures. Separately, Chalmers announced that the Australian Taxation Office would begin consulting on modernising Australia's business tax system—pre-filling contractor income for sole traders to save an estimated 400,000 hours and $37m in costs each year—and simplifying minor benefits rules by scrapping assessments of small benefits below $300. Coles chief executive Leah Weckert noted that cost-conscious families were swapping to cheap protein sources such as mince or eggs, with spaghetti bolognese remaining a family staple.
items.title: RBA Dissenters Warn of Sharper Downturn as Inflation Stays Elevated

items.summary: At a royal commission into alleged corruption across Victoria's construction sector, Bandidos member and former CFMEU organiser Joel Leavitt gave evidence that he could not recall why union representatives were pushing hard to have him hired on a construction project. Leavitt confirmed acting as a health and safety representative on building sites for the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU), though he denied being placed there by the union, telling the commission that you get onto a site only when told to come by the builder rather than through CFMEU membership. Messages between Leavitt and former CFMEU organiser Gerry McQuaid suggested some resistance from the builder to hire him while he was publicly associated with outlaw motorcycle gangs; in one message McQuaid wrote they were pushing hard but might drag it out for another week or two, which counsel assisting Chris Carr SC asked about before Leavitt clarified that 'pushing' meant speaking to the builder. Commissioner Chris Kourakis AC suggested McQuaid may have been pushing for Leavitt's work on a Laing O'Rourke job in Cranbourne, south-east of Melbourne, from March to August 2021, possibly because he had use for him there; Leavitt said that was the organisers' role and conceded his gang association carried notoriety at the time. The first two weeks of hearings centred on a two-day June 2022 standoff between the CFMEU and construction management over the Gap Road level crossing removal at Sunbury, north-west of Melbourne; during this sensitive round-the-clock work stage when the rail line was temporarily closed at great cost to the project, the union forced work to halt after issuing dozens of safety notices that bosses argued were disingenuous. On the second day, construction bosses met with union representatives Joe Myles and Paul Tzimas at the union's headquarters and agreed to demands including installing union-aligned labour, traffic management and health and safety representation on site.
items.title: CFMEU Pushed to Hire Notorious Bandidos Member on Construction Project; Royal Commission Hears of June 2022 Sunbury Standoff

items.summary: Malaysian actor and filmmaker Hans Isaac announced his engagement to former Miss Universe Malaysia Francisca Luhong James, 31, following a marriage proposal in Paris. The 55-year-old shared the news on Instagram on Monday (Nov 16), posting photos of the couple posing with the Eiffel Tower while showing off her engagement ring. Writing 'Forever with my favourite person,' Isaac described proposing to Francisca as the 'best decision' he had made, joking that she is now stuck with him. According to Malaysian publication New Straits Times, the couple have known each other for six years and began dating more seriously earlier in 2026. They are reportedly planning to marry in mid-2027, with a traditional engagement ceremony scheduled for January. Isaac currently chairs Malaysia's National Film Development Corporation (FINAS) and has spent more than two decades in the entertainment industry as an actor, director and producer. He is known for films including Buli (2004), Baik Punya Cilok (2005) and Cuci (2008). His bride-to-be, Francisca, 31, is a model and former beauty queen from Kuching, Sarawak who made history in 2020 as the first Dayak woman to be crowned Miss Universe Malaysia. Of Kayan, Kenyah and Iban heritage, she represented Malaysia at the 69th Miss Universe pageant in Florida, USA, in 2021. Isaac was previously engaged to former beauty queen Aileen Gabriella Robinson in 2017, but the couple called off their engagement later that year.
items.title: Actor Hans Isaac Announces Engagement to Former Miss Universe Malaysia Francisca Luhong James

items.summary: The Japanese government and ruling parties are considering toughening taxation on short-term condominium resales, which are viewed as a factor driving up condo prices in Tokyo and other urban areas. Currently, the total tax rate on capital gains from individual resale is about 40% for properties held five years or less and about 20% for those held more than five years. The government plans to newly impose a 52% tax rate for properties sold within a year of acquisition, plus an additional tax equivalent to 10% of capital gains for companies making such short-term resales. It also intends to stop applying a special measure that lowers the real estate acquisition tax rate from 4% to 3% for newly built condominiums bought and resold within a year without being lived in. These tougher measures are expected to curb speculative transactions and will be included in a fiscal 2027 tax system reform package. According to Real Estate Economic Institute, the average price of newly built condo units sold in the Tokyo metropolitan area in the first half of fiscal 2026 was ¥114.94 million, exceeding the ¥100 million mark for the first time, while existing unit prices have also trended upward. At the same time, mortgage rates are rising with Bank of Japan interest rate hikes, making home ownership increasingly out of reach for the average household.
items.title: Japan Considers Higher Taxes on Short-Term Condo Flipping Amid Soaring Tokyo Prices

items.summary: China's tech capital of Shenzhen has adopted an unusual quiet as it prepares to host world leaders this week, banning car horns, grounding delivery drones, and urging residents to leave their vehicles at home. The meeting is the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit, which U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian leader Vladimir Putin will attend. Officials view the event as an opportunity for Shenzhen to showcase its transformation from an agricultural backwater into a high-tech, orderly city. More than 1.5 million local car owners have pledged to stay off the roads in exchange for APEC car stickers and, if they keep their word, transit cards worth up to 100 yuan ($15).
items.title: Shenzhen Hushes for Trump and APEC Summit

items.summary:
A boom in gold and critical mineral mining in Myanmar has triggered a transboundary pollution crisis, as heavy metals from unregulated mines contaminate multiple river systems shared with Thailand. Following Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow's Nov. 12 visit to Naypyidaw, where he spoke with the military regime about trade, border security and Thai river contamination, observers remain frustrated by slow progress on bilateral solutions and a lack of intervention from China, Myanmar's primary consumer of its critical minerals.

The crisis stems from an agreement signed in August that was heavily edited during negotiations. Sources within Thailand's foreign ministry confirmed to Mongabay that the joint working group born out of this agreement has not met once since it was signed Aug. 6. Civil society and government officials warned beforehand that revisions requested by Myanmar meant the bilateral efforts would likely fail for tens of thousands of downstream communities.

For nearly two years, Thai authorities have detected dangerous levels of arsenic and other heavy metals in the Kok, Sai and Ruak rivers — a three-river system feeding into the Mekong River — as well as within the Mekong's sediment. The Salween River has also been found contaminated at points over 20 months by chemicals linked to Myanmar mines.

The final agreement omits clauses that would have ensured joint water testing on transboundary waterways, called for joint investigations into pollution sources, and aimed to instate legally binding responsibility for polluters. It also prohibits international or regional technical assistance while binding both sides to secrecy about data generated through the agreement without explicit permission.

"The Myanmar side doesn't want to accept responsibility for the pollution," said Suebsakun Kidnukorn of Mae Fah Luang University in Chiang Rai, adding that she could not understand why Thailand accepted this. Pianporn Deetes, executive director of Rivers & Rights, called the final version "significantly weaker" than what Thailand originally proposed and warned it risks a public health disaster.

Contamination has left people on both sides of the border without access to water for drinking, bathing, cooking or farming, while damaging ecosystems and contaminating crops. A Mongabay analysis shows Myanmar's military controls land where just 577 of 2,245 identified mines have been located; the rest are in territory held by armed factions including the Kachin Independence Organization, the People's Defense Forces and the United Wa State Party.

Chinese trade data show imports of minerals worth $2.5 billion from Myanmar in the first nine months of 2026, of which rare earth elements made up $871 million. Thailand's re-exporting role has grown substantially — China imported $228 million's worth of minerals from Thailand January through September, compared to just $110 million in 2025.

Water quality testing results published on Sept. 21 by Thailand's Pollution Control Department show arsenic levels at six of the Kok River's 15 monitoring stations exceeded the national safety limit of 0.01 milligrams per liter from Aug. 3 to Aug. 7. In the Sai River, which flows less than 75 meters (246 feet) from where officials met in late August 2026, arsenic levels reached up to 0.284 mg/l — more than 28 times the safety limit.

The latest data on Oct. 29 shows dangerous arsenic persisted in Sai River samples through September 2026, resulting in raw water production and distribution being suspended by Chiang Rai's Provincial Waterworks Authorities on Nov. 5 as pollution overwhelmed filtration infrastructure. The problem has contaminated some 20,800 hectares (51,398 acres) of farmland across nine districts of Chiang Rai.

Preliminary findings from testing on some 200 soil samples found that 20% of farmland in the Kok, Sai and Ruak river basins were contaminated to dangerous levels with more than 25 mg per kilogram of arsenic; a further 50% require monitoring due to levels ranging from 14-25 mg/kg. Elevated arsenic has also been detected in the urine of Chiang Rai farmers.

Thailand's Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment acknowledged receiving but did not respond to questions, as did Myanmar's Press Office and Information Bureau of the President's Office. On Nov. 13, Thailand's Department of Primary Industries and Mines announced it was drafting a new law to tighten regulations on imports of antimony, copper, gold, lead and rare earth elements from Myanmar.

The same day, Thai PBS reported China was expected to sign an agreement with Mae Fah Luang University to increase water testing capacity in Chiang Rai. But residents demand solutions rather than more tests: "China must also be part of the solution," said Pianporn, a Chiang Rai resident. Neither Chinese Embassy in Bangkok nor Consulate in Chiang Mai responded.

Witthaya Masah, senior technical officer at Chiang Rai's Provincial Department of Fisheries, warned that if sampling from the Kok River was still possible, the Sai River was too dangerous to sample and predicted the Kok-Sai-Ruak ecosystem would be functionally dead within 10 years. Testing published on Sept. 21 showed arsenic levels in water samples exceeded safety limits at six stations.

The Subcommittee on Transboundary Water Pollution received updates from the Royal Irrigation Department and Provincial Waterworks Authority on their 2.2-billion-Thai-baht ($66 million) plan to fix pollution across three rivers through water processing plants, new tap water sources, a planned dam designed to filter heavy metals, and safeguarding uncontaminated resources.

Officials noted they were 100 million Thai baht (almost $3 million) short for their plans, with none beginning until next year. The Thai government's response has left communities across the country's north feeling forgotten, leading to a peace walk earlier this year aimed at reminding officials of challenges faced as a result of perceived inaction.

"The real test is not whether a document was signed, but whether contamination entering Thailand is actually reduced," said Pianporn. The challenge now is to identify responsible mining operations, stop further contaminant releases, enforce environmental standards and restore damaged ecosystems.
items.title: Thailand-Myanmar River Pollution Agreement Weakened; China Remains Silent on Transboundary Mining Crisis

items.summary: A technical issue at JPMorgan Chase has disrupted online banking across the United States financial system, with thousands of customers reporting difficulty accessing their accounts and using Zelle on Monday. The largest US bank by total assets attributed the problem to a software bug affecting its internal hardware systems, which caused transaction delays while it worked to restore services; some Chase customers received messages stating that certain services were temporarily unavailable. Other banks such as Bank of America and Citigroup were not independently affected but may have experienced slowed transactions when interacting with Chase or routing Zelle payments involving Chase accounts. Zelle itself was reported fully operational by Early Warning Services, the Arizona-based company owned by a group of financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo. Chase spokesperson Joe Evangelisti explained that other banks were impacted only to the extent they participated in transactions with Chase. The outage was not caused by a cyber attack but rather an isolated incident tied solely to the bug, and Chase said customers retained access to their accounts and funds while expecting resolution by end of day Monday. Separately, officials confirmed this disruption was unrelated to last week's Microsoft outage during an upgrade that affected Outlook, Teams and Copilot for hours, as well as Friday's air traffic control failure that grounded all US flights due to a malfunctioning router overwhelming the aging system.
items.title: Online Banking Delays Hit Major US Banks Amid JPMorgan Chase Software Bug

items.summary:
French President Emmanuel Macron is visiting Malaysia for a two-day trip to Kuala Lumpur, marking his first visit since 2017. The visit comes ahead of the countries' 70th anniversary of diplomatic relations, with both sides seeking to upgrade their relationship into a strategic partnership. Macron will meet Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on Tuesday to discuss strengthening cooperation in defence, trade, energy transition and critical minerals.

Malaysia's foreign ministry said the meeting would focus on upgrading ties into a strategic partnership that provides a framework for deeper cooperation across key areas, with both nations aiming for mutually beneficial partnerships. Macron and Anwar are also expected to witness an exchange of several memoranda of understanding (MoUs) on Tuesday in areas of strategic cooperation.

A central theme of the visit is diversifying France's sources of rare earths, which are essential for manufacturing magnets used in electric vehicles and electronic devices. Macron emphasized that having multiple supply sources reduces the risk of halting production lines due to parts shortages and allows greater certainty about investing and producing in France. This effort comes as Western nations seek to reduce their reliance on China, the world's largest rare earths producer.

Following an initial partnership deal signed in July 2025, French firm Carester and Malaysian miner Malaco have agreed to cooperate on a rare earths mining and processing project. The collaboration includes a separation plant in Malaysia's Perak state that can process an estimated 13,000 metric tons of rare earths annually, according to Carester chief executive Frederic Carencotte.

France is also offering assistance with Malaysia's energy transition plans and its efforts to move from advanced semiconductor packaging to chip design. French Ambassador Marc Abensour noted the two countries are ready to deepen cooperation across a wide range of defence sectors, including industrial partnerships and countering emerging hybrid threats such as cyberattacks and disinformation.

France's push for closer defence ties arrives amid Malaysia reassessing its foreign suppliers after Norway revoked an export licence for missiles destined for its naval fleet. The move has raised questions about the trustworthiness of international partners, particularly those from Western or NATO countries.
items.title: Macron Visits Malaysia as France Seeks Closer Defence and Rare Earths Ties

items.summary: President Donald Trump departed the White House on Monday, turning his attention from a nationwide ground stop that snarled air traffic toward economic deals and what he called historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The planned summit in Shenzhen was described by China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning as of 'groundbreaking significance,' aimed at safeguarding world peace, while Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov indicated a one-on-one Trump–Putin meeting was being arranged. Trump framed the agenda around nuclear disarmament with Russia and China, plus discussion of Iran, but he also said he would raise Ukraine's war in which he claimed 'Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers [per month],' even though administration officials had earlier signaled they would steer clear of that conflict. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced concern about the gathering, warning against a repeat of the 1945 Yalta Conference and its division of Germany; he cautioned 'We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence.' Trump also floated meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his China visit. The trip began in Manila before continuing to Shenzhen's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and included Elon Musk of SpaceX and Tesla as an adviser on the flight.
items.title: Trump heads to Asia for historic nuclear talks with China and Russia amid domestic turmoil

items.summary:
The United States is still recovering from a nationwide flight shutdown triggered on November 13, 2026 by a telecommunications failure in its air traffic control (ATC) network. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a ground stop that lasted nearly five hours after the failure disrupted communications and radar data across the ATC system — the longest nationwide shutdown since the September 11 attacks in 2001. Although the stop was lifted later that evening, airline operations remained affected over the weekend; more than 11,500 flights were canceled or delayed on Sunday alone. Cancellations fell unevenly across carriers: about 28% of JetBlue flights and 20% of American Airlines flights were canceled, while United Airlines, Southwest and Delta reported cancellations of just 3% to 5% of their flights.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said flights were expected to fully return to normal by Monday. He told ABC's "This Week" that there was no evidence of a cyberattack or malicious intent, pointing instead to a problem during a routine upgrade at an FAA telecommunications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. The FAA contractor L3Harris had been replacing aging copper telephone lines with fiber for new routers; the newly installed routers began flooding other routers with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. To stabilize the network, the FAA disabled the broadcasting function on 69 similar routers across the national airspace system.

The root cause remains under investigation as officials examine whether it stemmed from faulty equipment or an installation error by the contractor. Duffy acknowledged that some affected routers were purchased in 2001 and obsolete by 2006 yet remained in service, underscoring broader aging-infrastructure concerns. A September 2024 report by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) found that of the FAA's 138 air traffic control systems, 51 were unsustainable and 54 potentially unsustainable — meaning 105 systems, or over 76%, faced sustainability risks; of those 105, 58 had critical operational impacts on airspace safety and efficiency. The GAO reported that 73 of these systems were deployed more than 20 years ago, with 40 over 30 years old and six more than 60 years old. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford noted in September that more than 300 of the agency's ATC facilities operated as technological silos, some still relying on decades-old computers unable to communicate seamlessly.

This is not the first such disruption: in January 2023 a failure in the FAA's Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system disrupted more than 11,000 flights, and in September of this year a telecommunications circuit failure at an ATC facility in Philadelphia caused around 9,500 flight delays and cancellations. Airlines for America head Christopher Sununu — former Republican governor of New Hampshire — described the system as "held together with string and duct tape." Duffy had requested $30 billion from Congress to upgrade the system; after the shutdown his request rose to $50 billion.

The crisis quickly became a political blame game. Trump urged Congress on Truth Social to "give the money, FAST!" while blaming the Biden administration for leaving behind a deteriorating FAA system. Duffy acknowledged the shutdown occurred under his watch but declined to apologize, arguing he inherited decades of underinvestment and that the Trump administration was moving faster than predecessors; he called again for more than $50 billion for a full overhaul. Democrats pushed back, noting Congress had already approved $12.5 billion for upgrades while only about $1 billion had been spent, with Duffy defending the spending as committed to equipment expected by 2028 but insufficient for a new telecommunications network and software.
items.title: US Flight Shutdown Exposes Aging Air Traffic Control System and Sparks Political Blame Game

items.summary: The article frames robotics as an emerging frontier in global technological development that is generating new opportunities for innovation and industrial cooperation across the Asia-Pacific region. It identifies 3D sensing as a key technology within this field, noting that it enables machines to perceive their surrounding environment. The piece then focuses on Shenzhen, China, describing how a growing industrial ecosystem there is helping translate this 3D sensing technology from its component stage into real-world applications.
items.title: Vision of the future: Inside Shenzhen's robotics ecosystem

items.summary: Late Monday, Russian forces struck two major bridges crossing the Dnipro River in Kyiv, damaging critical infrastructure and causing water and power cuts in parts of the Ukrainian capital. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary information indicated hits on both the North and South bridges, adding that there were water and power cuts across portions of the city. The attacks came as Moscow launched a wider wave of drone and missile strikes across Ukraine, including in the regions of Cherkasy and Kharkiv. Reuters witnesses reported a series of loud explosions in the capital, though Reuters could not immediately independently confirm the reports. In the region of Cherkasy, a Russian missile attack injured three people, while Moscow also targeted Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-biggest city, according to local officials on Telegram. Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said intelligence showed Russia planned strikes for Monday evening and throughout Tuesday. Separately, Zelenskiy noted that Ukraine had held new online talks with US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as well as European representatives, on the prospects of ending the war with Russia — progress was reportedly made toward an agreement, though important challenges remain to end the conflict that Russia started by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Moscow annexed the Black Sea Crimea peninsula in 2014.
items.title: Russian strikes hit two key bridges in Kyiv, disrupting water and power supplies

items.summary:
According to CBS News, a senior White House official confirmed that Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk would be part of President Donald Trump's presidential delegation traveling to Asia but would not participate in the meeting between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin scheduled for Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. The issue of Iran is expected to feature prominently in these trilateral discussions, with a senior US official indicating that Trump intends to raise the matter directly with both Chinese and Russian leaders. Speaking on condition of anonymity about this intention, the same official told reporters that "the president does intend to talk about Iran." The meeting would mark the first gathering between the three leaders and is expected to focus primarily on reducing nuclear weapons proliferation, even as ongoing conflicts in Iran and Ukraine remain among broader geopolitical concerns. Trump himself described denuclearization as a "tough subject" when speaking to reporters before departing for his Asia tour on Monday.

Trump's Asia tour unfolds against continuing geopolitical tensions and Washington's efforts to engage Beijing and Moscow on nuclear arms control and international security issues. The US President is scheduled to first visit the Philippines, where he will participate in the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and hold discussions with regional leaders. On Tuesday, Trump is expected to meet leaders of India, Japan, and Australia under the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad), marking the first in-person Quad leaders' summit in two years and the first during his current presidential term; these discussions are expected to focus on regional security and cooperation in the Indo-Pacific. Trump is also scheduled to sign a trade agreement with Thailand and attend a dinner with Southeast Asian leaders, followed by a state visit and luncheon banquet hosted by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the presidential palace before departing for Shenzhen.

During his China visit, Trump is expected to participate in the APEC summit and hold bilateral discussions with Xi before joining Chinese and Russian presidents for the trilateral meeting. He also indicated the possibility of meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his Asia tour, although no formal meeting has been confirmed. In remarks delivered before boarding Marine One at the White House, Trump characterized the trip as a "big trip," noting engagements in the Philippines focused mostly on economics but touching other matters, followed by time with President Xi and plans to meet President Putin, while acknowledging that he may also meet Kim Jong Un. Meanwhile, senior members of the Trump administration, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, are accompanying the President. This visit comes against a backdrop of broader US-China trade and technology tensions, including concerns surrounding Nvidia's advanced semiconductor exports to China; however, White House officials said this issue was not expected to dominate discussions during the visit.

The Asia tour is expected to conclude after Trump's engagements in China, with the US President also referring to the upcoming G20 summit in Miami in December as another major diplomatic engagement. The article was published on November 17, 2026.
items.title: Elon Musk Expected to Accompany Trump on China Visit; Iran on Agenda for Trilateral Talks with Xi and Putin

items.summary:
A new OpenAI study finds that 98 per cent of surveyed scientists expect artificial intelligence to accelerate discoveries in their fields, underscoring the growing role of tools such as ChatGPT in research. The findings draw on an analysis of 580,186 scientific messages from 1,819 researchers and a survey of 251 scientists using OpenAI's ChatGPT for Academic Researchers programme. Scientists estimate that AI lets them complete tasks at the same quality level in nearly half the time, with more than one in five believing a discovery normally taking 10 years could be achieved within three years. Reading and writing together accounted for more than half of the average scientist's messages, while AI was used across stages including reviewing literature, writing, analysing evidence, developing software, and generating research ideas.

The report notes that human involvement remains essential: researchers sought clarification, checks or revisions after around 32 per cent of AI responses. At the same time, bottlenecks persist — limited time or staffing was cited by 51.8 per cent of respondents as a constraint, while 43.8 per cent pointed to funding; only 6.4 per cent reported having no major bottlenecks. OpenAI said that translating productivity gains into faster discoveries will also depend on funding, staff and the capacity to conduct experiments.

The study was published November 17, 2026.
items.title: OpenAI Study: 98% of Scientists Expect AI to Accelerate Discoveries

items.summary: In October 2026, India's retail inflation rose to 6.09 per cent, breaching the Reserve Bank of India's upper tolerance limit of 6 per cent for the first time as CPI inflation crossed the 6% mark (s87). The RBI's target is 4 per cent with a two-percentage-point band on either side, and inflation targeting was formally institutionalised in 2016 to maintain price stability while keeping growth objectives in mind. Food prices were the sharpest pressure point: food inflation reached 8.94 per cent (up from 7.74 per cent in September), with rural food inflation at 9.09 per cent versus 8.68 per cent urban, and overall retail inflation running higher in rural areas at 6.63 per cent compared with 5.41 per cent in cities. Wholesale prices fared worse: WPI inflation surged to 12.29 per cent (from 11.39 per cent in September), its highest level since the 2022-23 base series, driven largely by fuel and power inflation of 32.84 per cent, with primary articles at 9.24 per cent and manufactured products at 9.54 per cent.
items.title: India's October 2026 Inflation Crosses RBI Tolerance Limit: What It Means for Consumers and the Outlook

items.summary: An estimate by market intelligence firm EIIR Trend, shared with Economic Times (ET), suggests that last week's Microsoft outage could have dealt a roughly $200 million hit to the Indian information technology services industry. The study estimates this against an overall sector size of about $315 billion for India's IT services industry. According to the cited analysis, the loss of connectivity through the affected enterprise suite left IT services companies facing lost billable hours, delayed project execution, and additional costs related to delivery commitments.
items.title: Microsoft Outage's $200 Million Billing Blow to India's IT Services Industry

items.summary:
A report alleges that Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, worked in parallel toward the same objective of advancing China's AI capabilities ahead of the United States. According to The Wall Street Journal, a review of Chinese public records showed that Kang built a large network of government-backed data centres across China during the period his wife was involved with Jensen Huang, then Nvidia's CEO. As described by the WSJ, Alice Huang's role was reportedly to cultivate a relationship with Jensen Huang that eventually turned romantic and to help secure a supply of Nvidia's advanced computing chips, which Washington has sought to keep out of China; Kang's role was to build out the data-centre network. The WSJ had earlier reported that Kang introduced his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he reportedly knew for about a decade, and sometimes joked with associates that she was the Nvidia chief's personal assistant — details the paper said it could not confirm with Kang himself.

The Financial Times separately reported that in early 2025 the couple sought investors for a Southeast Asian data-centre project worth several hundred million dollars. They reportedly told investors that obtaining Nvidia chips would be no problem and that Alice Huang did not disclose any close relationship with Jensen Huang. The FT also reported that Kang sits on the board of Guilin Bank, a state-backed lender.

On unconfirmed details and denials, The New York Times said it could not confirm whether the two are legally married, though Kang has been introduced as her husband to investors and colleagues. US intelligence officials reportedly suspect Alice Huang of working for China's Ministry of State Security; China has denied the allegations, and she has not been charged with any wrongdoing.

In fallout at Nvidia, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last week, and the company's board hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate whether his conduct compromised national security or company secrets, per CNBC. President Donald Trump recently said that nobody had proven Alice Huang was a spy.
items.title: Alice Huang's Husband Built a State-Backed Data-Centre Network in China While She Was Involved With Nvidia's Jensen Huang: Report

items.summary:
US President Donald Trump said he would be fine with Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia's chief executive, noting that the tech leader had learned a hard lesson from his recent controversy. The remarks came after reports that Huang had assembled a group of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his comeback. Huang stepped down last Friday following revelations of several extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia client whom US intelligence reportedly suspects is working for Beijing.

Trump pushed back on the characterization that Alice Huang was a spy, saying he did not know whether she was and that nobody had proven it. He acknowledged that Jensen Huang should not have behaved as he did in his personal life but treated that as separate from any professional concerns, adding that he had heard of no national security issues linked to the relationship.

On the broader chip issue, Trump noted his administration had barred Nvidia from selling its most advanced chips directly to China. Critics pointed out that Nvidia can still sell certain AI chips there under an arrangement giving the US government a share of revenue, and Chinese firms face no current restriction on renting chips housed in data centres across Southeast Asia. Huang said he did not expect to raise either Huang or chip sales in his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, adding he did not want to insult China just before arriving.

Despite Trump's support, Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back, a source told CNBC on Monday.
items.title: Trump Backs Jensen Huang's Reinstatement as Nvidia CEO Despite Affair and Espionage Controversy

items.summary: A senior Reserve Bank of India official reiterated the central bank's demand that Tata Sons, the holding company of the conglomerate spanning salt to software, be listed in accordance with existing regulations. A Deputy General Manager in RBI's Department of Regulation wrote a letter on Monday responding to a communication from Tata Sons Pvt Ltd dated October 6, advising compliance with all applicable rules governing non-banking companies in the upper layer, including listing requirements. The bank first pressed for a listing when it rejected Tata Sons' application to de-register as an NBFC on September 11, ahead of a board meeting on September 17 that surfaced divisions at the group's higher echelons. Noel Tata, half-brother of Ratan Tata and current chair of Tata Trusts—which owns over two-thirds of Tata Sons—opposes the listing, viewing it as a threat to the Tata way of working, while management led by N Chandrasekaran believes compliance with the law is necessary. Shapoorji Pallonji Group, the largest private owner in Tata Sons with an 18 per cent stake, supports a listing because it would help raise liquidity to clear its substantial debt.
items.title: RBI Reiterates Demand for Tata Sons Listing Amid Deepening Group Rifts

items.summary: According to a report cited by Fox News on Monday (local time), Nvidia's board is not considering bringing back former chief executive Jensen Huang, who resigned on November 12 after approximately three decades—33 years—at the helm of the multi-trillion-dollar chipmaker. The decision comes amid an independent board investigation into his departure and growing efforts to reinstate him: prominent technology executives are reportedly mobilizing support for a comeback campaign that has drawn backing from major shareholders, including Elon Musk, who signed an open letter urging the board to bring Huang back. Trump weighed in before departing for the 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila on Monday (local time), expressing openness to Huang's return while cautioning against aggressive posturing that could "insult China" ahead of his scheduled trip to Shenzhen and a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit. His remarks contrasted with those of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who argued Sunday that Nvidia needed a dramatic shake-up under an outside chief executive and demanded answers about whether restricted US AI chips had been diverted to Beijing amid allegations involving alleged relationships within the company, including one with an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed accused of spying for China. On succession, Nvidia's board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm and had not formally engaged any candidates; Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas—leader since 2022 of the SoftBank-backed British chipmaker—is emerging as one name under consideration, though he previously worked at Nvidia around seven years more than a decade ago. Meanwhile, Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO following Huang's departure.
items.title: Nvidia Board Rules Out Jensen Huang's Return as CEO: Report

items.summary: The Nvidia board is not considering bringing founder and former chief executive Jensen Huang back as CEO, according to a person familiar with the matter. The company has engaged law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead an investigation into Huang's conduct, examining whether his behavior compromised US national security or Nvidia's trade secrets. Huang resigned from the company he founded last week, ending a 33-year tenure at its helm. His departure followed less than a week after acknowledging having an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for an Nvidia customer and is alleged to have had contacts with Chinese intelligence as well as employees at the chipmaker. The situation has prompted calls from segments of the technology industry for his reinstatement, including an online petition that attracted 180,000 signatures and backing from figures such as Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. Meanwhile, Nvidia's board is proceeding with selecting a search firm to identify candidates for the role, with a representative confirming on Friday that it was in the process of engaging such a firm.
items.title: Nvidia board declines to revive Jensen Huang's CEO return amid security probe

On Monday, November 17, customers at several of the largest US banks encountered difficulties accessing their accounts online. Downdetector.com reported service disruptions across multiple major financial institutions and payment platforms, including Bank of America, Chase, JP Morgan, US Bank, Wells Fargo, and Zelle. Per AP, some Chase users attempting to log in received an error message stating that certain services were unavailable while the company worked on resolving them. At the time of publishing, Downdetector recorded approximately 2100 reports for Bank of America customers and nearly 5000 reports for consumer banking company Chase, covering issues such as account balances and transactions, web login, transfers, and wires. AP cited a Chase spokesperson describing the disruption as a technical bug rather than a cyber issue; due to this problem, some transactions were taking longer than usual to complete, though customers retained access to their accounts and funds while efforts continued to resolve it quickly.

These banking disruptions followed a major Microsoft outage from last week that disrupted widely used services including Outlook, Teams, and the AI assistant Copilot for hours. Microsoft apologized for the global disruption to its 365 services, which occurred on Thursday, November 12, 2026, and continued into Friday. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, shared a Preliminary Post-Incident Report explaining what went wrong.

According to Lamanna, three primary issues converged to knock offline the networking gateway that sits in front of many Microsoft 365 services: higher load combined with lower server capacity caused the gateway to trigger a latent bug from July. Requests built up until the servers stopped responding entirely. The failure occurred during the peak window of traffic in the US, and recovery took longer because servers returning into service were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again.
items.title: US Banks Face Online Outage Days After Major Microsoft Disruption

items.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi of India and US President Donald Trump will participate in the Quad Leaders Summit held alongside the ASEAN-India and East Asia summits in Manila. This marks the first Quad meeting since September 2024, taking place during ongoing bilateral trade negotiations between India and the United States. Discussions at the summit are expected to cover supply chains, maritime security, critical minerals, and artificial intelligence across the Indo-Pacific region. The gathering also underscores India's trade and cultural ties with Southeast Asia while supporting New Delhi's Act East and SAGAR initiatives.
items.title: Modi and Trump to Attend Quad Leaders Summit in Manila Amid Trade Talks

items.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited the Gurudwara Khalsa Diwan in Manila, Philippines, where he offered prayers at the Sikh place of worship. He described himself as 'very blessed' to be there and shared his visit on social media platform X, expressing gratitude for the opportunity to pay respects at the gurdwara. The trip was part of his delegation's attendance at the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in the Philippines. The item is written by Pranjal Pandey, a journalist with the editorial desk of The Times of India (Online), who focuses on the implications of global events for India, particularly geopolitics and defence.
items.title: PM Modi Visits Gurudwara Khalsa Diwan in Manila Ahead of 49th ASEAN Summit

items.summary: An IndiGo aircraft operating on the Bengaluru sector from Mangaluru aborted its take-off at approximately 6.05 pm on Monday, subsequently returning to the bay while carrying 229 passengers and seven crew members. Following a detailed technical inspection by the airline's engineering team, the aircraft was declared Aircraft on Ground (AOG), and all passengers deboarded. The airport and airline teams were present to assist passengers and address their queries. IndiGo later arranged a ferry flight from Bengaluru; 34 of the original 229 passengers travelled on it with the relief aircraft leaving Mangaluru Airport at 12.10 am on Tuesday, according to sources. A source clarified that the aircraft in question was not airborne. Two incidents of technical glitches in aircraft have been reported in the state in a single day.
items.title: IndiGo flight to Bengaluru aborts take-off at Mangaluru Airport

The article reports that actor Robert Pattinson has been announced as the new James Bond, or 'Double Oh Seven,' an unexpected choice given his reputation for playing eccentric, unconventional characters such as vampires and Batman. At 40 years old, he is described as slender in physique and reputed for portraying shapeshifters and outliers, making him the single-most eccentric pick for the role despite a cult following and unimpeachable acting talent. The upcoming Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve—also helming Pattinson's forthcoming Dune: Part Three—and written by Steven Knight of Peaky Blinders fame. There is no clarity yet on when the movie will be released.

The piece traces James Bond's history, noting that he was created by British writer Ian Fleming in 1953 and first portrayed on screen by Sean Connery in Dr No in 1962. Bond has long symbolized Englishness for nearly as long as Queen Elizabeth II. The most recent Bond film before this announcement was released in 2021, when Daniel Craig's version of the character appeared to be concluded with 'No Time to Die.' Since then, the franchise—though a money-spinner and pop culture juggernaut—has been overtaken by other franchises such as Tom Cruise's Mission: Impossible films and Matt Damon-led Jason Bourne movies. Earlier Bond eras led by Roger Moore between 1973 and 1985 were seen as easily ridiculed, while Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan somewhat steadied the franchise afterward.

Daniel Craig revived interest in Bond with his brooding portrayal beginning with Casino Royale in 2006, renewing attention for at least four more releases. In 2022, Amazon MGM Studios acquired the James Bond intellectual property, signaling its belief that the character is not done yet and its aim to align Bond with contemporary thinking on heroism and villainy through Villeneuve and Pattinson's casting.

The article cautions that appearances can be deceptive when millions of dollars and fan expectations are involved. Independent-minded filmmakers like Sam Mendes (Skyfall, Spectre) and Cary Joji Fukunaga (No Time To Die) only tweaked the formula slightly. Hollywood has changed drastically since 2021, with five years having wrecked certainties about public taste; there is no guarantee that a storied franchise will automatically attract audiences or that righteous heroes punishing designated 'bad guys' will be readily accepted. Bond films have also competed against espionage dramas on streaming platforms that emphasize psychological aspects over flashy fights and reject the notion that the West knows best.

The production promises to be unpredictable, with Villeneuve's serious approach and Pattinson's manner potentially creating either a match made in oddball cinema or a disastrous punt. Some risk has been lowered by Villeneuve's well-received Dune films and Pattinson's recent mainstream turn, including The Batman (2022), whose sequel is expected in 2028.

Pattinson could be nominated for an Oscar for any of his roles, having starred as a groom-to-be in 'The Drama,' a reality show host in 'Primetime,' and a nobleman in 'The Odyssey.' He is well placed to carry Bond's iconic elements—sharp suits, wry British humour, insouciant rule-breaking. The article poses open questions about whether Pattinson might swap the Aston Martin db10 for an EV bike or a martini for an India Pale Ale; whether Villeneuve and Knight will acknowledge that in the age of Donald Trump, Elon Musk and Gaza, real adversaries lie in Washington DC, Silicon Valley and Tel Aviv; and whether the 'Bond girl' trope might be banished. The mission to reimagine Bond's arc is likely impossible, but the film could also become something James Bond has never been: atypical.
items.title: Robert Pattinson as James Bond: A Maverick Takeover of a Storied Franchise

items.summary: In an interview with The Wire, writer and peace-and-justice activist Harsh Mander argues that contemporary India has entered a new age of unreason that runs counter to centuries of scientific temper and rationalism. He notes that although the phrase “scientific temper” does not appear in the preamble of India’s constitution, it was embedded as a fundamental duty under Article 51A(h) only in 1976; historian S Irfan Habib contends that the idea nonetheless informed many debates in the constituent assembly and the preceding anti-colonial struggle. Mander rejects the assumption that “scientific temper” is Nehru’s coinage, tracing its popular use to late-19th- and early-20th-century thinkers such as Bertrand Russell, who described it as critical undogmatic receptiveness; for modern India, however, it was Jawaharlal Nehru who most eloquently championed the concept. In his 1934 essay “The Past and the Present,” Nehru identified the absence of reason and its consequence—bigotry—as chief enemies to be fought wherever found, insisting that no tradition making one a prisoner of mind or body is ever good. Mander stresses that scientific temper is not opposed to religious faith but battles blind superstition; it incorporates both inquiry against unreasoning dogma and humanism, and cannot be reduced to technocratic faith in science alone. He warns that today’s education system deprives young people of critical imagination while encouraging uncritical faith in inherited tradition, producing bigoted thinking. Drawing on Habib’s survey of India’s civilisational history, Mander highlights ancient sceptical traditions—the Buddhists, Digambara Jains, Samkhyas, Saugatas or Mimamsakas and the Charvakas philosophers around 600 BCE—and medieval rationalist voices such as Amir Khusrau, Basava/Basavanna of the 12th century (who spoke of human equality irrespective of caste), Kabir of the 14th- and 15th-centuries, Guru Nanak, Emperor Akbar’s emphasis on reason being supreme, social reformers Ram Mohan Roy in 1804 and Jotirao Phule, who founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (Truth-Seeking Society) in 1873; Swami Vivekanand linked rationality to modernity; Rabindranath Tagore invoked a “heaven of freedom” where reason has not lost its way and rebuked Mahatma Gandhi for calling the 1934 Bihar earthquake divine chastisement over untouchability. During constituent-assembly debates, Mander points to Maulana Abul Kalam Azad and Ambedkar as leading rationalist voices; influenced by John Dewey, Ambedkar saw modern science as a democratising force that replaced theological foundations with testable experience. Anand Teltumbde is quoted on the courage of challenging hegemonic social order while condemning Hindu and Muslim communalists as unmodern. Mander laments India’s descent into an age of unreason in which BJP leaders, affiliates and even occasionally the prime minister invoke myths—Shiva placing an elephant head to replace Ganesh’s decapitated one, the Mahabharat being “webcast,” pushpak vimans as ancient airplanes—as evidence of ancient scientific advance. He cites V Kamakoti, director of India’s Indian Institute of Technology Madras, recounting a story in which fever reportedly disappeared within 15 minutes after drinking cow’s urine (gomutra), promoted today for antibacterial and digestive uses. The age of unreason has also produced killings of rationalists—Narendra Dabholkar in 2013; Govind Pansare in February 2015; M. M. Kalburgi in 2015; journalist Gauri Lankesh in 2017—none brought to justice. Quoting Habib, Mander warns that the crisis is not only religious bigotry but the spread of a culture of ignorance threatening science’s future, and declares the battle for scientific temper “a battle for the soul of India.” He identifies himself as founder of Karwan e Mohabbat and visiting faculty in Heidelberg University’s South Asia Institute. The piece closes with Mander noting that Russell embraced Einstein’s relativity because it was evidence-backed yet not dogmatic; even Newton could be overturned, underscoring reason’s enduring value against superstition and unreasoning acceptance of received doctrine.
items.title: Harsh Mander: India’s New Age of Unreason and the Legacy of Scientific Temper

items.summary: On November 17, Brent crude futures fell 64 cents (0.7%) to $91.8 a barrel while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures dropped 55 cents (0.6%) to $85.17, continuing the week's declines of 16% and 13%, respectively. The benchmarks' softness reflects growing expectations that global supply will outstrip demand. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), average oil supply in Q4 would reach roughly 105 million barrels per day—about 1.7 million bpd above forecast demand, marking a shift from its earlier expectation of a fourth-quarter deficit as Middle East exports recover faster than global consumption despite ongoing attacks on shipping. Traders are now contemplating excess supply for the first time since the US-Iran conflict began, and analysts note that this narrative change is dampening market tone; KCM Trade's Tim Waterer observed that while the geopolitical risk premium from the US-Iran conflict has not vanished, it is taking a back seat as attacks on Gulf infrastructure and shipping in the Strait of Hormuz persist. Looking further ahead, Goldman Sachs expects Brent to average $88 a barrel next year before easing to $78 by end-2027 as supply disruption risks remain but the risk premium normalizes. Citing Goldman analysts including Daan Struyven via Bloomberg, crude supply is projected to exceed end-use demand by 2 million barrels per day in 2027 even after accounting for potential disruptions of half that magnitude. The brokerage's base case assumes Middle Eastern supply would rise above its 2025 average—supported by ship-to-ship transfers and pipeline additions—while production growth elsewhere stalls, leaving the market caught between elevated supply disruption risks and industry adaptability.
items.title: Oil Prices Ease as Supply Surplus Hopes Grow; Goldman Sachs Forecasts Lower Brent Through 2027

items.summary: Spot gold was little changed at $3,856.52 per ounce by 0028 GMT after hitting its lowest level since October 2025 on Monday. US gold futures for December delivery rose 0.2% to $3,859. Bullion sank to a one-year low on Monday, battered by high Treasury yields, a strong dollar and expectations of tighter monetary policy, putting it on course for further losses and its worst year in more than a decade. The dollar rose to its highest level since April 2025, supported by last week's strong inflation data and hawkish Fed commentary; a stronger dollar makes greenback-priced bullion more expensive for overseas buyers. Markets see a 96.6% chance of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, while the probability of a larger 50-basis-point move is priced at 3.4%, according to CME's FedWatch tool. Elsewhere, Bank of Japan hawkish board member Hajime Takata said its policy rate must rise to a good position early and focus on mounting inflation risks, signalling a possible hike as soon as December. Among other metals, spot silver steadied at $47.05 per ounce, platinum gained 0.1% to $1,450.75 and palladium rose 0.1% to $969.75.
items.title: Gold Near One-Year Low as Strong Dollar and Fed-Hike Bets Weigh

items.summary: The sons of imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan have accused authorities of subjecting their father to prolonged physical and mental torture at Adiala Jail, warning that he could die in custody without urgent medical intervention. In an interview with Sky News's Mark Austin, Sulaiman Isa Khan and Kasim Khan expressed concern over the deteriorating health of the 74-year-old Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder, alleging that he was being kept in solitary confinement for 22 to 23 hours a day, with little human contact and no access to independent medical care. The brothers said prison authorities had instructed guards not to speak to their father, adding that the isolation was being used to exert psychological pressure on him. They alleged that authorities had failed to implement an August 18 Supreme Court order directing that Khan be shifted to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical examination and treatment, with increased family access including regular telephone conversations with his sons. The brothers said nothing has changed despite the court order from August, and his health continued to deteriorate; Sulaiman Isa Khan noted his blood pressure is now dangerously high at about 193. Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges through an open letter seeking urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife, Bushra Bibi, saying doctors had warned of the risk of a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest. However, Pakistan's cabinet minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry disputed Khan's claims, saying he had received regular medical attention and been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations, while the government rejected allegations of solitary confinement and denied that Khan was being denied access to his family.
items.title: Imran Khan's Sons Warn Ex-PM May Die in Custody Without Medical Care

items.summary: The Kerala High Court permitted the medical termination of a pregnancy exceeding 27 weeks for a 15-year-old rape survivor, with Justice Harisankar V Menon ruling that she should not be forced to continue the pregnancy given the trauma from her assault. Although a medical board had unanimously recommended delaying termination or delivery until after 32 weeks—citing an exceptionally high risk of severe health complications associated with extreme premature birth, including cerebral palsy, visual impairment, and severe intellectual and developmental disabilities—the court nonetheless allowed immediate termination without delay. The Kerala government was directed to arrange the procedure promptly following a written undertaking from the girl and her parents confirming their willingness. The state must also provide neonatal care if the baby survives; if complications arise as the medical board warned, necessary aid shall be provided 'as and when it arises.' Additionally, should the child survive but not be kept by the survivor, she must unconditionally surrender the infant for adoption. If the fetus does not survive termination, the state is required to preserve tissues and blood samples—including DNA, fingerprinting, and mapping—since an FIR has been registered.
items.title: Kerala High Court Approves Abortion for 15-Year-Old Rape Survivor Beyond Medical Board's Recommendation

items.summary: The Election Commission of India (ECI) told the Supreme Court, via an affidavit filed after a new senior deputy election commissioner joined on November 2, that its Information Technology department was placed under fresh oversight through a work order dated November 4. This reorganization followed a controversial July 28 order issued by Maneesh Garg — which had prompted two election commissioners to write to the cabinet secretary objecting to the changes — and ECI stated that this earlier order was never implemented because of a subsequent July 30 order recalling it. The new arrangement assigns director general of IT Seema Khanna, who is at the centre of allegations that ECI centralised digital voter roll infrastructure and imposed software restrictions preventing state officials from accessing voting lists, to be supervised by senior deputy election commissioner Pawan Kumar Sharma. Meanwhile, Maneesh Garg retained election planning duties but will now be assisted by deputy election commissioner Prakash Rajpurohit, who also holds charge of delimitation. In its affidavit, ECI acknowledged that problems in the SIR process were bound to arise due to the large number of voters and fully digitalised data, affirming its commitment to ensuring eligible voters appear on voter lists while inconsistencies are addressed.
items.title: Election Commission of India Reorganizes IT Oversight After Digital Voter Roll Controversy

items.summary: A passenger bus travelling from Haridwar to Chamoli lost control around 4:30 am near Gular market and veered off the road over the Gular bridge into a roughly 100-metre-deep ravine in Uttarakhand's Tehri district early on Tuesday morning. The crash killed eight people, with another 26 injured; rescuers extricated all 26 survivors from the mangled vehicle and carried them up the steep slope to the roadhead on stretchers before shifting them by ambulance to nearby hospitals for treatment, while the bodies of the eight deceased were recovered for post-mortem examination. A State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) team from the Byasi post launched rescue operations upon receiving the alert, with additional teams dispatched from the Dhalwala post and battalion headquarters given the severity of the crash; SDRF Commandant Arpan Yaduvashi described an intensive joint operation conducted alongside local police, administration officials, and residents after rescuers braved difficult terrain and adverse conditions. A thorough search confirmed no passengers remained trapped before the operation concluded. The article notes a broader pattern: more than 1,000 road accidents are reported in Uttarakhand every year, worsened by treacherous, winding, narrow mountain roads that become even more hazardous during monsoon and winter seasons when poor visibility compounds the danger. In response to this recurring problem, the Uttarakhand cabinet approved the Road Safety Policy, 2025 in February 2025, with a goal of reducing road accidents by 50% by 2030.
items.title: Bus Plunges Into 100-Metre Gorge in Uttarakhand's Tehri; 8 Killed, 26 Injured

items.summary: According to CNN, US intelligence has picked up reports that Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or chemical weapon inside the United States. The report cited seven officials and said the plotting has been very specific, including locations and targets within Washington, DC. However, sources told CNN that these potential attacks represent options rather than an indicator of imminent threat, with no evidence suggesting Iran has decided to move forward; whether it even has personnel in place to execute such a plan remains debated. US intelligence views active planning for unconventional weapons on its own territory as a signal of alarming willingness to escalate by Iran. Officials feel the country is vulnerable to dirty bombs—devices that package radioactive materials into conventional explosives and can spread radiation across blocks or miles—which are easy to assemble and could be carried out by someone already living inside the US, exploiting porous borders over roughly ten years. The report came days after an Iranian diplomat on X threatened harm against two US Navy personnel blamed for a Tomahawk missile attack that killed more than 150 people, mostly students, in Minab on February 28 during the opening hours of the US-Israeli war.
items.title: US Intelligence Warns Iran Is Planning Dirty Bomb and Chemical Attacks on Trump Officials in Washington

Two Christian organisations in West Bengal have asked state BJP president Samik Bhattacharya to identify the missionary schools and individuals he accused of involvement in religious conversions and anti-India activities, and to make evidence supporting his allegations public. The letter from the Bangiya Christiya Pariseba and the West Bengal Association of Christian Schools followed remarks attributed to Bhattacharya at a programme marking tribal freedom fighter Birsa Munda's birth anniversary at Kolkata on Sunday (November 15). Samik Bhattacharya alleged that religious conversions were taking place in Asansol, accused the principal of an elite college in Kolkata of involvement in such activity, claimed a school had objected to a woman employee wearing saffron saris because she attended BJP meetings, and said an official at a Kolkata school had kept a Pakistani flag in his chamber. He also warned that missionary schools involved in what he called anti-India activities would not be allowed to operate, and accused some institutions of retaining a British-era mindset more than seven decades after independence.

Bhattacharya did not name the institutions behind these allegations. In their letter on Monday, the two organisations said they could not independently verify the authenticity of the viral video containing his remarks. But they expressed concern over the statements attributed to him, saying broad allegations without identifying the institutions unfairly cast suspicion on the entire Christian community and the more than 800 educational institutions it operated in the state. The letter is signed by founding state secretary and spokesperson of the Pariseba Herod Mullick and secretary of the WBACS Fr Moloy D'Costa.

The organisations asked Bhattacharya to name the schools, colleges and individuals concerned and place any supporting evidence in the public domain. They also sought an impartial investigation into the alleged incidents and legal action against anyone found guilty of using force, deception or inducements to secure religious conversions. They said they did not support unlawful conversions and would condemn any institution or individual found guilty of such activity. Their objection, they said, was to generalising allegations against the wider Christian community without identifying those accused.

The letter also questioned the suggestion that missionary institutions continued to harbour a colonial mindset. It said Christian schools and colleges had served the country for more than two centuries and educated generations of Indians, including prominent political leaders. The organisations' appeal came amid a series of complaints by Christian groups about attacks on churches, prayer meetings and worshippers in different parts of Bengal since the BJP came to power in May.

Pariseba recorded 48 incidents of alleged attacks and intimidation over five months and said only 16 first information reports (FIR) were registered. The figures were cited by its founding secretary at a prayer rally in Kolkata this month. The organisation also rejected allegations that its prayer gatherings were being used for forced conversions, saying such claims had repeatedly been used to disrupt prayer meetings and justify attacks.

The Pariseba had earlier submitted complaints to the National Human Rights Commission, the West Bengal Human Rights Commission and the National Commission for Minorities, seeking an independent investigation into the incidents and action against those responsible. The CPM's Sujan Chakraborty described Bhattacharya's remarks as an attack on the Constitution and the education sector, while Trinamool Congress MP Dola Sen and Congress leader Soumya Aich Roy also criticised the BJP leader's statements.
items.title: Christian groups challenge Bengal BJP chief to name schools behind conversion claims

On Tuesday, November 17, petrol and diesel prices remained unchanged across major Indian cities even though the Centre raised export levies on diesel and aviation turbine fuel (ATF). The Finance Ministry increased the special additional excise duty on diesel exports to ₹14 per litre from ₹11.50 in an order issued late Monday, while it left both petrol and domestic-market diesel duties unchanged; consequently Indian consumers were largely shielded from price shocks stemming from a recent surge in global oil prices amid the Middle East conflict.

Union Minister Suresh Gopi said that an immediate cut in fuel prices was not technically possible because oil companies are currently incurring losses worth ₹42,000 crore and there is "chaos" in petroleum supply. Speaking at Meenambakkam airport, he noted that while individual states could reduce petrol taxes, the financial position of oil companies had to be considered before any immediate reduction.

Separately, global crude prices declined on Tuesday amid expectations of a global supply surplus as recovering Middle East exports eased concerns over supply disruptions despite continued attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures fell 44 cents (0.5%) to $92 a barrel and WTI futures dropped by the same amount to $85.28 a barrel at 0102 GMT.

The International Energy Agency said last week that the global oil market was expected to return to surplus in the fourth quarter of this year as Middle East exports recover faster than demand, while US Strategic Petroleum Reserve inventories fell to 276.4 million barrels — their lowest level since August 1982 following a commitment to release 172 million barrels from the reserve.
items.title: Indian Fuel Prices Hold Steady as Global Crude Slips; Government Raises Diesel Export Levy Amid Oil Company Losses
